expected_evidence: Archaeological settlement-pattern continuity/discontinuity data (Clovis-age site density, radiocarbon date distributions) across the ~10,950 BCE boundary in North America
Ancient/modern DNA studies testing for a population bottleneck or founder-effect discontinuity in Native American lineages around the Younger Dryas onset

Geological impact-proxy layers (black mat, platinum anomaly, nanodiamonds, microspherules) at multiple North American sites, and whether their stratigraphic position correlates with any demographic decline
Faunal extinction/turnover records (megafauna decline timing) compared against human occupation intensity as an independent demographic proxy
Astronomical/geophysical modeling or crater/airburst-signature searches assessing whether an airburst event of demography-altering scale is physically plausible at this date
Comparative regional archaeological surveys (lithic technology continuity, e.g., Clovis-to-Folsom transition) used to argue for or against population disruption
Model-prior literature synthesis from the ongoing Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis debate (Firestone et al. vs. critics) as a low-tier corroborating/refuting source
response.rationale:
Interval -10950 sits at the Younger Dryas onset boundary, so I use the 'younger-dryas' period row rather than 'upper-paleolithic' since the mechanism (cosmic-airburst) and claimed demographic effect are specifically tied to that boundary event debated in the YDIH literature. Relevant evidence kinds are geological (0.65) and astronomical (0.7) — both fairly detectable, since impact-proxy stratigraphy and airburst physics have been actively searched for across dozens of North American sites over the past two decades — plus material/archaeological (0.35) and genetic (0.3), which are much harder to resolve because Paleoindian population reconstructions from sparse site counts and ancient DNA are noisy and low-resolution at millennial timescales. Model-prior (0.3) reflects that this whole topic (YDIH) is a contested, unresolved debate in the literature I recall, not a settled fact, so any claim I make about it should be flagged as low-confidence. Averaging across the evidence kinds most relevant to testing a demographic 'refutation' claim (material, genetic, geological, astronomical, model_prior) gives roughly 0.45, meaning: if this refutation is true, we would plausibly have been able to detect supporting evidence (settlement continuity, absence of a genetic bottleneck) via archaeology and genetics, though not with high resolution — so a lack of decisive evidence in either direction should be partly attributed to the moderate-to-low detectability of demographic signals in this period rather than treated as proof the refutation is false. Geological/astronomical impact evidence is more robustly detectable and has in fact been the primary battleground of the actual YDIH debate.</rationale>
